course: Embedded Electronic Engineering Lab A — HW/SW Codesign
topic: Cross-Traffic RSU Controller: UPPAAL → C → FreeRTOS + VHDL

entries.objective: Clarify the Week 4 milestone task and required outputs.
entries.prompt: Check the professor's course instruction file and explain what Week 4 requires for the cross-traffic RSU project. Focus on HW/SW codesign, FreeRTOS, ModelSim, mapping from models, and repository/report deliverables.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI summarized that Week 4 is a proposal for HW/SW codesign and that Week 5 is the implementation split: software with FreeRTOS and hardware with ModelSim. It also identified that the project must keep a well-defined mapping from UPPAAL/C models to implementation artifacts.

actions: Compared the answer with the uploaded ESLabA instruction slides, especially the organization slide listing Week 4 as HW/SW codesign proposal and Week 5 as codesign implementation.
Checked that the instruction mentions C-code with FreeRTOS, ModelSim, GitHub, and a written report chapter.

issues: The answer initially used the broader phrase 'implementation' for Week 4, but the course slide makes clear that Week 4 is the proposal and Week 5 is implementation.

entries.reflection: This helped keep the milestone scope realistic: we should propose the partition and interface now, not claim that the full FreeRTOS/VHDL implementation is already finished.

entries.objective: Connect Weeks 1–3 artifacts to the Week 4 proposal.
entries.prompt: Using our previous requirements, UPPAAL model, and deterministic C core, write a concise recap of what is being partitioned in Week 4.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed a recap: Week 1 requirements, Week 2 UPPAAL model with Vehicle and RSU_Controller, Week 3 deterministic C core, then Week 4 partitioning without changing the verified safety contract.

actions: Checked the recap against the actual Week 4 proposal structure and the course milestone list.
Verified that the partitioning explanation does not introduce new traffic behavior that was not in the UPPAAL/C model.

issues: Some wording was too strong about complete verification; it was revised to say that six queries were checked in the model and runtime assertions were used in C.

entries.reflection: The recap made the report more traceable because it explains that the codesign proposal is based on already existing models instead of being a separate new design.

entries.prompt: Suggest a codesign methodology for deciding which RSU functions should remain in software and which should move to hardware.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested the criterion: keep irregular, stateful, control-heavy, frequently changing logic in software, and move regular, parallel, timing-critical conflict checks into hardware.

actions: Compared the suggested criterion with the functions in the C core.
Confirmed that conflict checking is pure Boolean logic while scheduling, queues, timers, and priority policies are stateful and branch-heavy.

issues: The answer was generic at first, so it was rewritten with the specific function names from our RSU controller.

integration.section: Section 3 Codesign Methodology and Partitioning Rationale

entries.reflection: This became the main scientific argument for the proposal: the split is based on computation type, not only convenience.

entries.prompt: Which parts of the RSU controller should stay in FreeRTOS software and why? Use the actual functions requestVehicle, grantVehicle, finishVehicle, priorityValue, betterPriority, existsBetterGrantable, and emergencyWaiting.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI classified scheduler loop, V2I/I2V/V2V messaging, state update functions, timers, priority scan, emergency hold, and aging as software because they are sequential, stateful, and policy-dependent.

actions: Compared the classification with the Week 3 C code structure and with the Week 4 report text.
Checked that every software component maps to either a FreeRTOS task, queue, timer, mutex, or shared state update.

integration.section: Section 3.1 Parts that stay in software; Section 4.1 Software part

entries.reflection: This clarified why FreeRTOS is suitable: it can represent vehicle tasks, RSU task, queues, delays, and policy updates.

entries.prompt: Which parts of the RSU controller should move into VHDL hardware and why? Focus on conflict(a,b), conflictsWithCrossing(i), and noCollision().
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI identified conflict checking as a good hardware kernel because it has no internal state, no timers, and can evaluate the 15 pairwise conflict cells for N=6 in parallel.

actions: Manually checked N=6 gives N*(N-1)/2 = 15 pairwise combinations.
Checked that the hardware proposal only moves conflict/capacity checks and not policy decisions.

issues: The AI first described the hardware as if it decided the whole grant. This was corrected so the hardware only returns safe_to_grant and safety monitor bits.

integration.section: Section 3.2 Parts that move to hardware; Section 4.2 Hardware part

entries.reflection: This changed the design from an unrealistic all-hardware scheduler to a cleaner coprocessor architecture.

entries.prompt: Explain how canGrant(i) should look after the hardware coprocessor is introduced, and show which checks remain in software versus hardware.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed a canGrant(i) wrapper: waiting state, emergency waiting, hardware safe_to_grant, and existsBetterGrantable. It explained that safe_to_grant replaces the conflict-related part of capacityAvailableFor(i).

actions: Verified that waiting and emergency policy are still software checks.
Verified that M/M/1 and M/M/2 capacity/conflict conditions can be represented in one hardware status bit.
Checked that priority ordering is not hidden inside the hardware block.

entries.reflection: The wrapper made the interface easy to understand in the report and separated safety gating from scheduling policy.

entries.prompt: Create a minimal register interface between the FreeRTOS RSU task and the VHDL Conflict & Safety Coprocessor.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed STATE_VEH[i], MODE, CAND, CTRL, ST_SAFE, ST_NOCOL, ST_CWC, and ST_ALARM registers, with directions and bit widths.

actions: Checked every register against data needed by the conflict function: origin, turn, emergency, crossing, MM_MODE, and candidate id.
Confirmed that status bits are sufficient for safe_to_grant, noCollision, conflictsWithCrossing, and collision alarm.

issues: The first suggestion had too many debug registers; it was reduced to a small interface that fits the proposal better.

entries.reflection: The register table gave the hardware/software boundary a concrete form and made the proposal more implementable.

entries.objective: Map UPPAAL/C constructs to HW or SW.
entries.prompt: Build a table that maps UPPAAL/C constructs to the proposed Week 5 implementation partition and gives one reason for each mapping.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI generated a mapping table for conflict, conflictsWithCrossing, noCollision, capacityAvailableFor, priority functions, canGrant, Vehicle FSM, RSU_Controller, and communication channels.

actions: Checked that each model function has exactly one primary implementation location.
Checked that the mapping satisfies the professor's requirement for well-defined mapping from models to implementation.
Revised rows where the AI mixed hardware and software responsibility too broadly.

integration.section: Section 7 Partition Mapping (UPPAAL / C → HW or SW)

entries.reflection: This table became the strongest traceability element from the verified model to the codesign proposal.

entries.objective: Represent UPPAAL vehicle templates in FreeRTOS.
entries.prompt: Explain how each UPPAAL Vehicle automaton location and clock can be represented in a FreeRTOS task.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI mapped Idle, WaitingInQueue, V2V_Enter, Crossing, and V2V_Leave to a vehicle task FSM, with period and crossTime represented by FreeRTOS timers or vTaskDelay.

actions: Checked the mapping against the UPPAAL vehicle state names used in the report.
Verified that committed enter/leave transitions are modeled as immediate task steps and not as extra waiting delays.

entries.reflection: This made the software design understandable for readers who know the UPPAAL model but not the FreeRTOS implementation.

entries.objective: Represent UPPAAL communication channels in FreeRTOS.
entries.prompt: Map req[], emg_req[], grant[], leave[], i2v_yield, v2v_enter, and v2v_leave into FreeRTOS communication mechanisms.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested using FreeRTOS queues for request/grant/leave messages and task notifications or one-to-many notifications for broadcast-like V2V/I2V events.

actions: Checked the proposal against FreeRTOS concepts already taught/used in the course context.
Compared the mapping with the RSU message paths in the architecture diagram.

issues: The term 'broadcast queue' was avoided because FreeRTOS queues are normally point-to-point; the final text says one-to-many notifications for broadcast behavior.

entries.reflection: This improved the design because it explains how communication semantics move from UPPAAL channels into RTOS mechanisms.

entries.objective: Define shared state and consistency mechanism.
entries.prompt: Explain how waiting[], crossing[], origin[], turn[], emergency[], crossingCount, and emergencyNotified should be shared between RSU task, vehicle tasks, and hardware.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed one shared-state structure protected by a mutex, with the RSU task as the main writer that mirrors the state into hardware registers before each decision.

actions: Checked that the state variables are exactly the ones used by the conflict checker and scheduler.
Checked that the risk of stale registers is addressed in the risk table.

issues: The first answer implied vehicle tasks directly update hardware registers; this was rejected to avoid state drift. The final design keeps the RSU task as the single hardware register writer.

integration.section: Section 4.1 Shared state; Section 10.2 Risks and mitigations

entries.reflection: This gave a clear mitigation for HW/SW consistency problems.

entries.objective: Handle M/M/1 and M/M/2 in the hardware status logic.
entries.prompt: Explain how MM_MODE affects safe_to_grant in M/M/1 and M/M/2 modes.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI stated that in M/M/1 safe_to_grant is true only when crossingCount is zero, while in M/M/2 it is true when fewer than two vehicles cross and the candidate does not conflict with current crossing vehicles.

actions: Checked against the queuing requirement from the course slides and the Week 4 proposal.
Confirmed that M/M/2 can allow V1 and V2 together only when no conflict exists.

entries.reflection: This connected the queuing requirement directly to the hardware status signal.

entries.prompt: Explain how emergency priority should be implemented in the FreeRTOS RSU task and how it interacts with the hardware safety check.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested that emergencyWaiting() remains in software and blocks non-emergency grants while an emergency request exists, while hardware still checks conflicts and capacity before any grant.

actions: Checked that emergency priority does not bypass noCollision or crossingCount.
Compared the design with the intended scenario where V0 emergency can pre-empt normal flow after yield notification.

integration.section: Section 4.1 RSU controller task; Section 5 canGrant; Section 9 verification plan

entries.reflection: This helped avoid a dangerous interpretation where emergency vehicles would always cross regardless of safety.

entries.objective: Document the V4/V5 critical conflict case.
entries.prompt: Explain why V4 north-right and V5 south-left must never cross together and how this should be checked in hardware and software.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI framed V4/V5 as a regression vector and linked it to the invariant A[] not(crossing[4] && crossing[5]). Hardware conflict cell (4,5) and software assertions should both reject the state.

actions: Checked the Week 4 proposal's critical-pair statement and verification table.
Planned a ModelSim test vector with both V4 and V5 crossing to verify that collision_alarm or noCollision failure is produced.

integration.section: Section 2 Recap; Section 9 Verification and Co-Simulation Plan

entries.reflection: This gave a concrete safety test instead of only a general no-collision statement.

entries.prompt: In the C simulation with strict static priority and continuous arrivals, V5 never crosses. Explain whether this violates safety and how to fix it.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI explained that starvation is a liveness/fairness issue, not a direct safety violation. It suggested adding aging so long-waiting vehicles get increasing effective priority.

actions: Checked the Week 3/Week 4 observation that V5 was not served even after extended simulation.
Confirmed that the original UPPAAL queries checked safety/reachability but did not guarantee bounded waiting for V5.

entries.reflection: This was an important correction: a design can be collision-safe but still unfair.

entries.prompt: Suggest a simple aging formula for priority comparison that can fix V5 starvation but does not override safety.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed maintaining age[i] while waiting[i] is true, resetting it on grant, and comparing priorityValue(i) - k*age[i) or an equivalent effective-priority value.

actions: Corrected the formula notation to priorityValue(i) - k*age[i].
Checked that aging is only applied after hardware safety gating and therefore cannot allow conflicting vehicles to cross.

issues: The AI's first formula contained a small bracket typo and did not clearly separate fairness from safety. The final text explicitly says aging only reorders safe candidates.

entries.reflection: This made the fairness improvement explainable without changing the VHDL conflict checker.

entries.prompt: Create a verification plan for the VHDL Conflict & Safety Coprocessor in ModelSim.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed a ModelSim testbench that feeds state vectors, checks noCollision and safe_to_grant against C reference outputs, and includes the V4/V5 conflict regression.

actions: Checked that every hardware output has at least one test: ST_SAFE, ST_NOCOL, ST_CWC, and ST_ALARM.
Added the requirement to compare against Week 3 C golden traces rather than only hand-written expected values.

entries.reflection: This gave the hardware part a measurable verification method, not only an architectural description.

entries.prompt: Can the hardware conflict checker be exhaustively compared with the C reference over all relevant reachable vehicle states?
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI reasoned that the input space is small because each vehicle only has limited origin/turn/emergency/crossing combinations, so exhaustive or near-exhaustive comparison is feasible for reachable states.

actions: Checked that the claim should be limited to reachable or project-defined origin/turn combinations, not every arbitrary 6-bit combination.
Revised the text to avoid overclaiming full formal proof of all possible road geometries.

issues: The AI initially implied full exhaustive verification over all possible traffic behaviors. This was narrowed to reachable state vectors for the project fleet.

entries.reflection: This improved scientific precision by limiting the claim to the model's defined state space.

entries.prompt: Explain what the FreeRTOS implementation should reproduce from the Week 3 C trace.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested checking that FreeRTOS reproduces the M/M/2 overlap of V1 and V2, the emergency V0 pre-emption after I2V yield, and the three safety assertions.

actions: Compared the proposed checks with the Week 4 verification table.
Added a log/counter based check for emergency V0 and M/M/2 concurrency.

entries.reflection: This made the software validation more concrete and linked it to earlier behavior.

entries.prompt: Explain how the FreeRTOS RSU task and VHDL coprocessor should be checked together.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI proposed that the RSU task writes the current state and candidate to the hardware register interface, reads hw_safe_to_grant, and the test fails if the hardware result disagrees with the C reference.

actions: Checked that the co-simulation criterion is binary and testable.
Added that ST_ALARM should be independent from the scheduling code, so safety violation detection does not depend only on software.

entries.reflection: This established a clear pass/fail rule for integration.

entries.prompt: List the main risks for the Week 5 HW/SW implementation and give realistic mitigations.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI generated risks: HW/SW state drift, interface overhead, ModelSim setup, aging breaking safety, and behavior drift from Week 3. It proposed mitigations using a single writer, mutexes, one-cycle register reads, early testbench setup, and golden vectors.

actions: Checked each risk against the architecture.
Removed speculative risks that were not connected to the actual implementation plan.

entries.reflection: This improved the proposal by showing that we know what can go wrong in Week 5.

entries.objective: Improve architecture diagram text and layout.
entries.prompt: Based on the current diagram, make the labels clearer and show the flow: Road and vehicles, Communication Layer, FreeRTOS software partition, VHDL hardware partition, and Verified Safety Contract.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI suggested a layered diagram with arrows for V2I/I2V/V2V messages, queue events, safe_to_grant, hardware monitor feedback, and safety assertions. It also suggested shorter labels to avoid overlap.

actions: Compared the generated diagram idea with the Week 4 proposal figures.
Manually adjusted label positions and shortened text boxes to avoid overlaps.

issues: The first diagram text was too crowded. Some labels were moved and shortened manually.

entries.reflection: The diagram became easier to explain to the professor because it separates road behavior, communication, software, hardware, and safety contract.

entries.objective: Revise proposal wording for scientific tone.
entries.prompt: Rewrite the Week 4 proposal in a professional but simple style without changing the technical meaning.
entries.ai_output_summary: The AI revised paragraphs for objective, partition rationale, safe_to_grant, verification, risks, and summary. The main technical terms were kept: UPPAAL, C core, FreeRTOS, VHDL/ModelSim, conflict matrix, safe_to_grant, and aging.

actions: Checked that the revised wording did not change the architecture or safety contract.
Manually edited the output to keep it consistent with the actual project assumptions.

issues: Some sentences were too polished and not close to the team's own style. They were simplified before integration.

entries.reflection: This helped make the report readable, but final responsibility remained with the team because the technical claims were checked and edited.

entries.objective: Generate AI usage protocol and BibTeX files.

entries.ai_output_summary: The AI produced a structured JSON protocol with 24 entries using the template fields: objective, AI tool, prompt, AI output summary, verification level/actions, evaluation status/issues/usefulness, integration, and reflection. It also generated a BibTeX entry that cites the machine-readable AI usage protocol.

actions: Checked the generated JSON against the uploaded protocol template fields.
Validated the JSON syntax using a parser.
Checked that the BibTeX entry includes the milestone, topic, course, protocol version, number of documented reasoning episodes, and JSON filename.

issues: The generated protocol is a cleaned documentation draft, not a literal raw chat export. It should be reviewed by the team before submission if exact prompt wording is required.
